entries.topic: Johnson inherits the Middle East: the "icebox" policy, Israel's tank request, and Eshkol's first official visit to Washington (November 1963–June 1964)

sources.label: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964–1968, vol. XVIII, Arab-Israeli Dispute, 1964–1967, volume summary, Office of the Historian
FRUS 1964–68 vol. XVIII, doc. 7: Memorandum for Record, "Israeli Arms Needs" (Komer; meeting of Harman, Gazit and Ron with Bundy and Komer)
FRUS 1964–68 vol. XVIII, doc. 65: Memorandum of Conversation, Johnson–Eshkol exchange of views, June 1964
FRUS 1964–68 vol. XVIII, doc. 66: Memorandum of telephone conversation, Komer and Under Secretary Ball, June 1964
FRUS 1964–68 vol. XVIII, doc. 68: Memorandum from Komer to President Johnson on the Eshkol visit, June 1964
Lyndon B. Johnson, "Remarks of Welcome at the White House to Prime Minister Eshkol of Israel", 1 June 1964, The American Presidency Project (UCSB)
Joint Statement following discussions with Prime Minister Eshkol, 2 June 1964 (text as republished by the Jewish Virtual Library)

William Burr and Avner Cohen (eds.), "Duplicity and Self-Deception: Israel, the United States, and the Dimona Inspections, 1964–65", National Security Archive, 10 November 2020 (republished by the Jewish Virtual Library)

claims.text: The State Department historians summarize Johnson's approach as continuing Kennedy's policy of good relations with both Nasser's United Arab Republic and Israel, and say that keeping the Arab-Israeli dispute "in the icebox" was central to it.

In a meeting recorded by Komer (it refers back to Eshkol's letter of 4 November 1963 and a meeting of 14 November 1963), Ambassador Harman, Minister Gazit and the military attaché Col. Ram Ron asked Bundy and Komer for surface-to-surface missiles, modern tanks and an answer to growing UAR naval strength, with tanks the immediate priority.

Israel's tank request in that meeting was to replace about 300 Shermans with 200 M48A3s and 100 M60s, then obtain about 200 more M60s over two to three years; the memo records defense at about 40% of Israel's regular budget and 11% of GNP.

Bundy told the Israelis that "in practical military terms Nasser's missiles were useless," warned that missiles added to Israel's "existing nuclear potential" could open a new dimension in the arms race, and said 1964 would be hard because of the pro-Israeli stance the US planned to take on the Jordan waters.

After an interagency review in early 1964 the US declined to sell tanks directly, because of its policy of not becoming a major arms supplier to the region, but agreed to help Israel obtain tanks from Europe.
Welcoming Eshkol on 1 June 1964, Johnson said it was "the first official visit by a Prime Minister of Israel" and pledged continued help "particularly in the field of desalinization of water."

In the recorded Johnson–Eshkol talks, Johnson said the US "could not provide tanks directly" but would help Israel get them elsewhere; Eshkol asked, "please do not push us into the Centurions"; Johnson said the US was "violently against nuclear proliferation" and "We back Israel fully on the Jordan water."

Komer told Under Secretary Ball that the President had told Eshkol "we could not give them but we would help all we could" on tanks, had raised Dimona, hoped Israel would "bite the bullet on the IAEA," and asked Israel not to "force us to say publicly that we are behind you."

The joint statement of 2 June 1964 restated US support for "the territorial integrity and political independence of all countries in the Near East," voiced concern at "the diversion of vitally important resources from development to armaments," and agreed joint studies on desalting.

Eshkol refused, on 3 March and 23 March 1964 and again in an April 21 reply, to let Washington reassure Nasser about Dimona; Johnson had written on 19 March that the danger was "a desperate pre-emptive attack"; Eshkol refused again on 1 June ("Why tell Nasser?") and conceded on 2 June after a private meeting, according to Komer's 3 June memo.

Komer judged the visit "a distinct plus": Israel agreed to let the US reassure Nasser on Dimona, to IAEA observers in a joint desalting study, to IAEA controls in principle on any large desalting reactor, and to seek IAEA agreement on its small reactor within nine months.

Johnson's letter to Nasser produced a July 1964 pledge that the UAR would not develop nuclear weapons; McCloy's September 1964 mission on missiles failed when Nasser said only a solution of the Palestine problem would end the arms race.

US relations with Cairo deteriorated over Yemen, the Congo and Vietnam: Congo-related aid ended in April 1965, the last P.L. 480 food funds were released in June 1965, and in June 1966 Rusk advised against renewing the P.L. 480 agreement, the US extending $70 million in food credit instead.

disputes.question: Did the June 1964 visit change US arms policy?

positions.view: The US record says no direct sale: Johnson told Eshkol the US "could not provide tanks directly" and would only help Israel get them from Europe.

The volume editors note that the European route (German tanks with US modernization kits) depended on secrecy and that within a year Washington was selling tanks directly, so the visit opened the road to the 1965 change.

entries.topic: The Arab summits of 1964 and the founding of the PLO: Cairo (January), the Jerusalem congress and charter (May–June), Alexandria (September)

sources.label: Final communiqué of the Council of Kings and Heads of State of the Arab League, Cairo, 13–17 January 1964 (English text, Economic Cooperation Foundation archive)
"Arab Summit Decides to Divert Jordan River", Jewish Virtual Library (from the Israel Ministry of Foreign Affairs)
Overall Chronology, Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question, Institute for Palestine Studies
Niyazi Gunay, "Arab League Summit Conferences, 1964–2000", Washington Institute PolicyWatch 496, 19 October 2000
The Palestine National Charter of 1964 (English text, Jewish Virtual Library)
Mouin Rabbani, "Does the 1964 PLO Charter Exclude the West Bank and Gaza Strip from Palestine?", 3 July 2025
CIA Office of Current Intelligence, memorandum on Palestinian organizations, 2 December 1966 (FRUS 1964–68 vol. XVIII; text via Jewish Virtual Library)

Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964–1968, vol. XVIII, Arab-Israeli Dispute, 1964–1967, volume summary

claims.text: Nasser invited the Arab heads of state to Cairo on 23 December 1963 to discuss confronting Israel's Jordan diversion project, which the Institute for Palestine Studies chronology says Israel had begun by the end of 1963.

The first Arab summit met at Arab League headquarters in Cairo on 13–17 January 1964; its communiqué condemned Israel's plan to "divert the course of the River Jordan" as a threat to Arab riparian rights, agreed to suspend inter-Arab media campaigns, and set the next meeting for August 1964 in Alexandria.

The communiqué spoke of "organizing the Palestinian people" so they could take part in liberating their country and affirmed "the sacred right of the Palestine Arab people to self determination"; it did not explicitly name a Palestinian entity.
The Cairo summit entrusted Ahmad al-Shuqairi with organizing the Palestinian people.

The FRUS editors record that King Hussein's 1964 request for US arms came under pressure from the Unified Arab Command, which an Arab summit had created; the GlobalSecurity account says the January 1964 Cairo summit created it under an Egyptian commander.

The first Palestinian National Congress met in Jerusalem on 28 May 1964 under King Hussein's sponsorship with nearly 400 appointed delegates; on 2 June it announced the PLO, approved a National Charter and a Basic Law, and elected Shuqairi president.

The 1964 Charter states: "Palestine with its boundaries at the time of the British Mandate is a regional indivisible unit" (Article 2); calls the 1947 partition and the establishment of Israel "illegal and false" (Article 17) and the Balfour Declaration and the Mandate "fraud" (Article 18); and says Jews of Palestinian origin "are considered Palestinians if they are willing to live peacefully and loyally in Palestine" (Article 7).

Article 24 of the 1964 Charter states that the organization "does not exercise any regional sovereignty over the West Bank in the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan," and names the Gaza Strip and the Himmah area in the same clause.

The second Arab summit, at Alexandria on 5–11 September 1964, recognized the PLO over Syrian and Saudi opposition, according to the IPS chronology; the Washington Institute dates its formal approval of the PLO to 11 September 1964.
The third summit, at Casablanca, ended on 18 September 1965 with no notable decisions, according to the Washington Institute survey.

A CIA memorandum of 2 December 1966 says the PLO was formed in 1964 with Arab League sanction, that Nasser had considerable influence over it, that its "Voice of Palestine" broadcast from Cairo, and that it tried to build a Palestine Liberation Army around Palestinian units in the Egyptian, Syrian and Iraqi armies.

In July 1966 Hussein withdrew official endorsement and support from the PLO, after friction over its taxing Palestinians and distributing arms in the West Bank and the camps; the PLO and the Syrian government then turned against him (GlobalSecurity account).

disputes.question: Did the 1964 Charter exclude the West Bank and Gaza from "Palestine"?

positions.view: Critics of the PLO cite Article 24 to argue that Palestinians did not claim the West Bank and Gaza before 1967.

Rabbani argues that Article 2 already defines Palestine as the whole Mandate territory and that Article 24 only defers to existing Jordanian, Egyptian and Syrian administration; the 1964 Charter was drafted by delegates chosen by Arab governments, and the 1968 Charter, drafted mainly by the guerrilla movements, dropped the clause.

disputes.question: Who created the PLO?

positions.view: The Arab League and Nasser: the CIA memo describes a League-sanctioned body under heavy Egyptian influence.
The IPS chronology stresses a Palestinian national congress in Jerusalem electing its own leadership, though with appointed delegates and under Jordanian sponsorship.

entries.topic: The National Water Carrier, the Arab headwater-diversion plan, and the Israeli strikes on the works (1964–1966)

sources.label: Aaron T. Wolf, Hydropolitics along the Jordan River (United Nations University Press, 1995), chapter "1964–1982: Water wars and territorial adjustments"
Ines Dombrowsky, "Die Wasserkrise im Nahen Osten", Aus Politik und Zeitgeschichte (bpb), 26 May 2002
Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964–1968, vol. XVIII, Arab-Israeli Dispute, 1964–1967, volume summary
FRUS 1964–68 vol. XVIII, doc. 65: Johnson–Eshkol memorandum of conversation, June 1964
FRUS 1964–68 vol. XVIII, doc. 7: "Israeli Arms Needs"
"Palestinian National Liberation Movement (Fatah)", Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question, Institute for Palestine Studies
"January 2, 1965 Fatah Raid", Center for Online Judaic Studies, citing Benny Morris, Righteous Victims, p. 364

claims.text: Under US mediation by Eric Johnston (1953–55), negotiators reached a technical plan in 1955 that Israel accepted; the Arab League declined to ratify it because a treaty with Israel would have meant recognizing it.

Wolf writes that Israel's National Water Carrier was supported "within the Johnston allocations" and that by 1964 enough of it was complete for diversions from the Jordan basin to the coastal plain and Negev to be imminent.

The Carrier entered operation in 1964, drawing from Lake Tiberias, which required lifting water from 212 metres below sea level; Wolf gives Israel's withdrawal as 320 million cubic metres a year from 1964.

At the January 1964 summit the options weighed were complaint to the UN, diversion of the upper tributaries, or war; a military assessment found the Arab states unprepared to defend diversion works, and the September 1964 summit chose diversion, financing works in Lebanon and Syria and helping Jordan build a Yarmuk dam.

The Arab plan, begun in 1965, would have diverted the Hasbani into the Litani in Lebanon and the Banias into the Yarmuk, impounded by a dam at Mukheiba, and could divert up to 125 million cubic metres a year; Lebanon stopped its part of the work in July 1965.

Israeli forces attacked the diversion works in Syria in March, May and August 1965, using long-range tank fire rather than artillery or aircraft, partly because of US warnings against preemptive action (Wolf).
The FRUS editors record that Washington asked Israel to pursue peaceful means on the Jordan waters rather than preemptive action.

Johnson told Eshkol in June 1964: "We back Israel fully on the Jordan water," and Bundy had earlier warned Israel that 1964 would be difficult because of the pro-Israeli stance the US planned to take on the issue.
The Banias diversion project was finally abandoned in 1966 (Dombrowsky); Wolf records border air battles in July 1966 and April 1967 as part of a "prolonged chain reaction of border violence".

disputes.question: How did Israel stop the diversion works?

positions.view: Wolf: long-range tank fire in March, May and August 1965, deliberately not air power.
Dombrowsky: Israel "bombed" the construction site several times shortly after work began.

disputes.question: What was the first Palestinian armed action against the Carrier, and whose was it?

positions.view: Wolf calls the 31 December 1964 attempt to sabotage the Carrier "the PLO's first action".
The IPS encyclopedia and Morris attribute the first operation to Fatah and date it 1 January (IPS) or the night of 2 January 1965 (Morris).

entries.topic: Palestinian citizens organize: al-Ard, its banning (1964) and the Yeredor ruling (1965)

sources.label: Yeredor v. Chairman of the Central Elections Committee for the Sixth Knesset, EA 1/65, Supreme Court of Israel (Versa, Cardozo School of Law)
Edo Konrad, "In Israel's democracy, dissent has always been off limits to Arab citizens", +972 Magazine, 17 November 2015
"Military rule" entry, Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question, Institute for Palestine Studies

claims.text: Al-Ard grew out of the "Popular Front" formed by nationalists and communists in 1959; Fouzi El-Asmar is named as one of its founders (Konrad).

Authorities closed successive versions of its newspaper and refused to register it as an economic company; its members were placed under surveillance, and some were jailed or banished to the Negev (Konrad).

The Supreme Court had held in HCJ 253/64, Sabri Jiryis v. District Commissioner of Haifa, that al-Ard sought to deny Israel's existence, and the Minister of Defense declared it an unlawful association (1964).

On 29 September 1965 the Central Elections Committee refused to confirm the ten-candidate Arab "Socialists' List" for the Sixth Knesset, on the ground that most candidates were al-Ard members and that "its initiators deny the integrity of the State of Israel and its very existence."

The Supreme Court, by majority (President Agranat and Justice Sussman), dismissed the appeal (EA 1/65; the decision was given on 12 October 1965, according to Justice Sussman's opinion), holding that the Knesset could not be used to pursue the state's destruction; Sussman described the approach as a "defensive democracy."

Justice Haim Cohn dissented: section 23 of the Knesset Elections Law said a duly submitted list "shall be confirmed," no statute empowered the Committee to reject it, and there was no "real, clear and present danger"; he wrote that the right to vote and be elected "is one of the fundamental rights of the citizen."
In 1963 an opposition motion to end military rule failed by one vote, two Arab members linked to Mapai, Jabr Muadi and Thiab Ubaid, voting with the government (IPS encyclopedia).

disputes.question: Was banning al-Ard a defence of the state or suppression of Arab political organizing?

positions.view: The Supreme Court majority: a list whose initiators deny the state's existence may be barred even without an express statute ("defensive democracy").
Justice Cohn in dissent, and Konrad writing in 2015: the rejection had no statutory basis, and the state treated secular Palestinian organizing as a threat regardless of ideology.

entries.topic: Bonn, the secret tanks and recognition: from the arms leak (October 1964) to diplomatic relations (12 May 1965)

sources.label: Marcel Serr, "Zur Geschichte der deutsch-israelischen Rüstungskooperation", Aus Politik und Zeitgeschichte (bpb), 30 January 2015
"Aufnahme diplomatischer Beziehungen zwischen der Bundesrepublik Deutschland und Israel", Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung, history calendar
"Dreieck Bundesrepublik – DDR – Israel", German Federal Archives (Bundesarchiv) theme article
FRUS 1964–68 vol. XVIII, doc. 99: Feldman, Bundy and Komer to Johnson, with Rusk's memorandum "FY-1965 Help to Israel" (October 1964)
Komer to Johnson, "U.S. Closes Deal on Tanks for Israel, Moves On to Planes", 29 July 1965 (Johnson Library; text via Jewish Virtual Library)
"Vor 70 Jahren: Der Deutsche Bundestag stimmt Luxemburger Abkommen zu", bpb, 16 March 2023
"Jordan: Development and Disaster", GlobalSecurity.org

claims.text: Shimon Peres and Franz Josef Strauss first met secretly in winter 1957 at Strauss's home in Rott am Inn; in August 1962 Adenauer approved a secret Israeli wish list worth 240 million DM, including tanks.

In October 1964 Rusk told Johnson that Israel would receive 150 M48A1 tanks from West Germany "as is" plus about 250 British Centurions; the covering memo by Feldman, Bundy and Komer spoke of "150 German M–48s, with an option on 82 more."

Under that arrangement the US sold kits to modernize the M48s (about $24 million) on MAP credit of 10 years at 3.5% with 10% down; "in the interests of secrecy" the tanks were to be fitted in Italy with diesel engines and larger guns, and Washington speeded replacement US tanks to Germany so the German ones could be released.
A letter exchange of 15 November 1964 provided that if the transaction became public before the US judged secrecy unnecessary, the US "might exercise its right of cancellation."

The deliveries became public in October 1964 (Bundesarchiv); Serr dates Egyptian press reports to autumn 1964, and says that after Nasser announced Walter Ulbricht's visit in January 1965 the Erhard government said it would stop arms deliveries to areas of tension, Israel included.
Ulbricht, the East German head of state, visited Egypt from 24 February 1965, received with military honours though without formal recognition of the GDR; Bonn then cut economic aid to Egypt.

On 7 March 1965 Chancellor Erhard announced immediate negotiations with Israel on diplomatic relations, using his authority to set policy guidelines without first informing the cabinet or Foreign Minister Schröder; his emissary Kurt Birrenbach learned of the decision from the Israelis in Tel Aviv.

The undelivered arms were converted into a payment of 140 million DM that let Israel buy weapons elsewhere (Serr); only 40 of the German tanks had been delivered, and in July 1965 the US agreed to sell 110 M48A2C tanks to replace the rest.
Diplomatic relations were established on 12 May 1965; the first West German ambassador, Rolf Pauls, presented his credentials to President Shazar on 19 August 1965.
Under the Hallstein Doctrine, in force since 1955, Bonn treated recognition of the GDR by a third state as an unfriendly act that could lead it to break relations.

The 1952 Luxembourg Agreement had committed 3 billion DM to Israel, 450 million DM to the Claims Conference and a 50 million DM special fund, paid partly in German goods such as ships, locomotives and factory machinery.

disputes.question: How did the Arab states respond to Bonn's recognition of Israel?

positions.view: Serr: thirteen Arab states withdrew their ambassadors from Bonn right after relations were established.
GlobalSecurity: Jordan joined nine other Arab states in breaking relations with West Germany in May 1965.

disputes.question: When did Ulbricht's Egyptian visit end?

positions.view: Serr: 1 March 1965.
Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung and Bundesarchiv: 2 March 1965.

entries.topic: Fatah's armed campaign: the first operation (January 1965) to the eve of the crisis

sources.label: "Palestinian National Liberation Movement (Fatah)", Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question, Institute for Palestine Studies
"January 2, 1965 Fatah Raid", Center for Online Judaic Studies, citing Benny Morris, Righteous Victims, p. 364
Aaron T. Wolf, Hydropolitics along the Jordan River (UNU Press, 1995)
Overall Chronology, Institute for Palestine Studies
CIA Office of Current Intelligence memorandum, 2 December 1966 (FRUS 1964–68 vol. XVIII)
Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964–1968, vol. XVIII, Arab-Israeli Dispute, 1964–1967, volume summary
"Jordan: Development and Disaster", GlobalSecurity.org
Report of the Secretary-General to the Security Council on the situation in the Near East, May 1967 (S/7896; excerpts via Jewish Virtual Library)

claims.text: Fatah's military wing, al-Asifa, launched its first operations in January 1965 (IPS chronology).

The IPS encyclopedia dates the first operation to dawn on 1 January 1965 against an Israeli water network, says Ahmad Muhammad Musa ("Salama") was killed, and notes that Palestinians mark the date as the start of their contemporary revolution.

Morris's account dates the raid to the night of 2 January 1965: a squad planted a charge by the National Water Carrier in the Galilee that was found and defused; returning, it was intercepted by a Jordanian patrol, its leader shot dead and the others arrested.
The FRUS editors record that Fatah incidents along Israel's borders, supported by Syria, increased from mid-1965, and that US officials opposed Israeli reprisals and urged UN action.

The CIA memorandum of 2 December 1966 says Israel attributed 61 sabotage incidents to Fatah since it emerged in January 1965; that Damascus gave it a base, training and a propaganda outlet; and that its money came mainly from wealthy Palestinians in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia.
The same memorandum says infiltrations were launched from Jordanian and Lebanese territory "without the approval of either the Jordanian or the Lebanese government."

Fatah and the PLO raided Israel without clearance from the Unified Arab Command or Jordan, which had tried to avoid incidents that invited reprisals; Israeli reprisals on West Bank targets grew harsher and more frequent from May 1965 (GlobalSecurity account).
In his May 1967 report U Thant called "El Fatah activities, consisting of terrorism and sabotage" a major factor in the tension.

disputes.question: When and how did Fatah's first operation take place?

positions.view: IPS encyclopedia: dawn, 1 January 1965, against an Israeli water network; Ahmad Musa killed.
Morris (via COJS): night of 2 January 1965; the charge was found and defused; the leader was shot after being intercepted by a Jordanian patrol.
Wolf: a failed sabotage attempt on the Carrier on 31 December 1964, described as the PLO's first action.

entries.topic: From the German route to direct sale: Jordan, the Harriman–Komer mission and the US–Israel memorandum of 10 March 1965

sources.label: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964–1968, vol. XVIII, Arab-Israeli Dispute, 1964–1967, volume summary
FRUS 1964–68 vol. XVIII, doc. 185: Telegram from the Embassy in Israel (Barbour) transmitting the signed memorandum of understanding, 10 March 1965
"Secret U.S.-Israel Memorandum of Understanding on Arms Sales" (10 March 1965), Jewish Virtual Library, citing the Israel State Archives
Komer to Johnson, "U.S. Closes Deal on Tanks for Israel, Moves On to Planes", 29 July 1965
Memorandum of Conversation, McNamara and Eban, 12 February 1966 (via Jewish Virtual Library)
FRUS 1964–68 vol. XVIII, doc. 273: Komer to Johnson, late February 1966

claims.text: In February 1965 the administration concluded that a tank sale to Jordan was necessary, because Hussein warned he would otherwise face pressure to accept Soviet aircraft, and sought to talk him out of supersonic jets; Eshkol's strongly negative reaction convinced policymakers that a direct sale to Israel would be needed (FRUS editors).

During the Harriman–Komer mission Israel resisted conditions linked to future arms, including nuclear inspections, a pledge on Jordan River water and referral to the UN; Johnson then offered a package (FRUS editors).

The memorandum transmitted by Ambassador Barbour on 10 March 1965 had the US reaffirm its concern for Israel's security and integrity, and Israel reaffirm that it "will not be the first to introduce nuclear weapons into the Arab-Israel area."

In the memorandum the US undertook to sell Israel "at least the same number and quality of tanks that it sells to Jordan," to complete the German M48 deliveries, and to help Israel obtain "a certain number of combat aircraft, if not from Western sources, then from the United States"; both governments agreed to full secrecy.
The FRUS editors summarize the aircraft clause as up to 24 combat aircraft and date Israel's nuclear reaffirmation to 11 March 1965.

The Jewish Virtual Library account, citing the Israel State Archives, presents the memorandum as the first US agreement to sell tanks to Israel directly and says it implied that Israel would not oppose US arms sales to Jordan.

On 29 July 1965 Komer told Johnson the deal was closed: 110 M48A2C tanks to replace the German ones and 100 M48A1 tanks to match those sold to Jordan, around $42 million over two years or more, plus conversion kits to fit 105 mm guns on the 40 tanks Bonn had delivered.
Komer added that Rusk was "strong against any US sale" of the 24 planes, "so we'll stall for a while and try to shift them to Europe."

disputes.question: What did Israel promise on nuclear weapons, and in what words?

positions.view: 10 March 1965 memorandum: Israel "will not be the first to introduce nuclear weapons into the Arab-Israel area."

Later US records use other wording: "not to be the first power in the Middle East to manufacture nuclear weapons" (McNamara to Eban, February 1966) and not to go nuclear "unless others do" (Komer, February 1966).

entries.topic: The first US combat aircraft: the A-4 Skyhawk decision and the Jordan F-104 balance (February–March 1966)

sources.label: FRUS 1964–68 vol. XVIII, doc. 270: Memorandum for Record, "President's Meeting on Israel/Jordan Matters", 12 February 1966
FRUS 1964–68 vol. XVIII, doc. 273: Komer to Johnson, late February 1966
Memorandum of Conversation, McNamara and Foreign Minister Eban, 12 February 1966 (drafted by Townsend Hoopes; text via Jewish Virtual Library)
Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964–1968, vol. XVIII, Arab-Israeli Dispute, 1964–1967, volume summary
"IAF retires Skyhawk after 48 years in service", Ynet News

claims.text: At a White House meeting on 12 February 1966 (Rusk, McNamara, Vance, Bell, Hare, Komer) the proposal was to sell Israel 48 aircraft centred on the A-4E and to offer Jordan "36 F–104s or F–5s"; McNamara ruled out the A-6 that Israel also wanted (cost about four times the A-4E, Vietnam shortages, a one-squadron force).

Johnson asked McNamara to tell the Israelis the decision was final, proposed trading aircraft and aid amounts for Israeli help in keeping Congress quiet about both sales, and said Congress was pressing him; he had already spoken to twelve congressmen and to Eban.
McNamara offered Eban 24 A-4Es with an option on 24 more (about $26 million for 24) on the Hawk terms of 10% down, 3.5% interest and 10 years.

The conditions McNamara set: Israel to keep relying mainly on Europe for aircraft, reaffirm its undertaking "not to be the first power in the Middle East to manufacture nuclear weapons," accept periodic inspection of Dimona, not use US aircraft as nuclear carriers, and keep full secrecy until Washington chose how to publicize.

Komer reported that Israel accepted: the US would sell "48 A4Es (about $50 million)"; Israel would quietly support selling 36 second-hand F-104s to Jordan (cash, 12 a year from 1968), reaffirm its pledge not to go nuclear "unless others do," and stop pressing for more aircraft for several years.
Hussein had asked for a quick answer, saying he would otherwise have to accept MiGs when Arab leaders met on 14 March 1966; Johnson approved proceeding.
The first four Skyhawks were unloaded at Haifa port on 29 December 1967, according to the Israeli Air Force as reported by Ynet.

disputes.question: Which aircraft did Israel get in 1966?

positions.view: The FRUS volume summary says "agreements were reached for the sale of 48 F–4s to Israel and 36 F–104s to Jordan."
The documents printed in the same volume (docs. 270, 273) and the McNamara–Eban record name the A-4E Skyhawk, 48 aircraft; the summary's "F–4" appears to be an error and should not be used.

entries.topic: Dimona under Johnson: the visits of 1964, 1965 and 1966, what they found and what they missed

sources.label: William Burr and Avner Cohen (eds.), "Duplicity and Self-Deception: Israel, the United States, and the Dimona Inspections, 1964–65", National Security Archive, 10 November 2020 (via Jewish Virtual Library)
"Duplicity and Self-Deception", James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies, 10 November 2020
FRUS 1964–68 vol. XVIII, doc. 298: Telegram 1085, State Department to Embassy in Israel, 11 June 1966
FRUS 1964–68 vol. XVIII, doc. 289: DIA Director Carroll to McNamara, "Preliminary Report on Visit to Israeli Atomic Energy Sites", 4 May 1966
"Israel and the Bomb: Highlights", National Security Archive (Avner Cohen)
Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964–1968, vol. XVIII, Arab-Israeli Dispute, 1964–1967, volume summary

claims.text: On 5 December 1963 Israel invited US representatives to visit between 10 and 15 January 1964; three US scientists spent one day, about eleven hours, at Dimona in mid-January 1964 and reported that "all significant facilities at this site were inspected."

The January 1964 team judged Dimona "an ambitious project" with a research purpose and estimated that without outside help Israel could not produce a first device until two or three years after deciding to.

For the next visit Eshkol first asked (October 1964) to postpone until after Israel's elections, then set 30 January 1965; on 4 January 1965 he rejected US terms of at least two full days, full access and independent measurements, insisting the team be "invited guests," not "inspectors."

The January 1965 team (Ulysses Staebler of the AEC, Floyd Culler of Oak Ridge, Clyde McClelland of ACDA) reported on 5 February 1965 that "nothing [at the site] suggests an early development of weapons program" and recommended visits "at intervals not to exceed one year."

In January 1965 Henry Kissinger met Israeli officials and scientists and told the US Embassy on 1 February that he had "a strong belief that Israel is already embarked on a nuclear program," naming Peres as "the strongest champion" of weapons as an absolute deterrent.

The embassy science attaché Robert Webber rejected the "bluff" theory (9 April 1965) and on 18 November 1965 said Dimona made "no sense except as the basis for a weapons project"; Burr and Cohen call him a rare exception among Johnson officials.

A three-man US team visited Israeli atomic sites from 31 March 1966 and reported "no evidence that Israel is producing or intends to produce nuclear weapons material"; it found Dimona running at much reduced power and no chemical separation plant there.

The same team could not account for 80 to 100 tons of uranium concentrate bought from Argentina, and could not determine whether a small separation plant existed elsewhere; it judged a concealed one could escape detection.

On 11 June 1966 Washington asked for visits every six months with full access to facilities and records, explaining that a reactor of Dimona's size could discharge a fuel load about every six months if the aim were weapons-grade plutonium, against about two years for peaceful use; Rusk had told Eban the issue was a "matter of fundamental significance" to the relationship.
Burr and Cohen write that the underground reprocessing plant was hidden from every US team and that none of the nine AEC teams that visited between 1961 and 1969 knew of it.

The National Security Archive summary says CIA reporting was never shared with the inspection teams, that by late 1966 CIA reports claimed a fully assembled bomb was weeks away (a view the State Department did not accept), and that Eshkol refused a nuclear test to preserve his understandings with the US.
The same summary reports Cohen's finding that Israel had improvised two nuclear devices and placed them on operational alert in late May 1967.
The FRUS editors record that Johnson's effort to secure IAEA inspection of all Israeli nuclear facilities failed and that Rusk warned in 1966 that Israel would "lose U.S. support" if it went nuclear.

disputes.question: Were the visits a real check?

positions.view: The teams of 1964, 1965 and 1966 reported no evidence of a weapons program, and the DIA wrote in May 1966 that no convincing intelligence contradicted them.
Burr and Cohen document Israeli limits on time and access and the concealment of the reprocessing plant from every team; Kissinger and Webber judged at the time that a weapons program was under way.

disputes.question: Dates of the 1966 visit

positions.view: State Department telegram of 11 June 1966: 31 March–1 April 1966.
DIA memorandum of 4 May 1966: 31 March–4 April 1966.

claims.text: After the coup of 8 March 1963, Amin al-Hafiz became the dominant figure from July 1963; between May 1964 and February 1966 power struggles between the Ba'th's centrist and leftist wings brought the Alawi generals Salah Jadid and Hafiz al-Assad to decisive power (Library of Congress).

On 23 February 1966 Jadid, Assad and Nureddin Atassi carried out a coup that put the more radical wing of the Ba'th in power (Library of Congress); GlobalSecurity calls it "the bloodiest of the many coups d'etat since 1949," with Hafiz wounded and arrested and Aflaq and Bitar expelled from the party.

Assad's appointment as defense minister was announced after the coup; on 1 March 1966 a government formed with Atassi as president and Yusuf Zuayyin as prime minister, while Jadid led through his party post.
A countercoup by the Druze officer Salim Hatum failed on 8 September 1966.
The CIA called Syria in December 1966 "the most bellicose Arab state" and said Damascus gave Fatah a base, training and a propaganda outlet.
Egypt and Syria signed a five-year defense pact in November 1966 (Library of Congress).
On 7 April 1967 an Israeli air engagement with Syria downed six Syrian fighter aircraft (Fanack); GlobalSecurity describes a land and air engagement on the border that day.
Laurens writes that the shooting down of six Syrian MiGs on 7 April exposed Nasser's inaction to his Arab critics.
The Library of Congress study says that in 1967 Israeli leaders repeatedly threatened to invade Syria and overthrow its government if raids across the Syrian border did not stop.

Tal records that Chief of Staff Rabin said the Damascus "authorities are behind the terrorists," which Tal reads as hinting at regime change, and that Eshkol warned "the last 14 incidents might lead us to take measures no less harsh than those taken on April 7th."

disputes.question: Who drove the Syrian front toward war in 1966–67?

positions.view: The Library of Congress study emphasizes Israeli threats against Syria; Laurens describes Rabin's "show of force" against Syria.
The CIA in December 1966 emphasized Syria's sponsorship of Fatah and called it the most bellicose Arab state.

entries.topic: Samu: the raid of 13 November 1966, the UN record, Washington's reaction and Resolution 228

sources.label: Report of the Chief of Staff of UNTSO (Lt-Gen Odd Bull) to the Secretary-General on the incident of 13 November 1966, S/7593

claims.text: The IDF archives describe Operation Magressa (13 November 1966) as a response to a Fatah mine attack near the West Bank border two days earlier that killed three Israeli soldiers on patrol; the CIA memorandum of 2 December 1966 says Israel attributed the 12 November road mining to the Palestine Liberation Front, and Rostow's 15 November memo also counts three Israelis killed.

Jordanian witnesses quoted by UNTSO said Israeli tanks crossed the line at about 05:45; UNTSO asked for a ceasefire by 08:55 without an Israeli reply, the Mixed Armistice Commission chairman called one for 09:45 that both sides accepted, and UN observers reached the scene at 10:35.

Force details in the UNTSO report come from Jordanian witnesses and were not independently verified: they describe about 80 M-48 Patton tanks, two columns of more than 40 half-tracks, 155 mm and 105 mm guns, and Mirage aircraft.

UN observers found at As Samu, a village of about 5,000 people in 1,200 houses, 125 houses completely demolished along with the clinic, a six-classroom school and a workshop, and one mosque and 28 houses damaged; 15 stone huts were destroyed at Kh. Jimba and the Rujm el Madfa'a police post almost totally destroyed.

The UNTSO report's totals give 3 civilians and 15 soldiers killed and 97 civilians and 37 soldiers wounded, while noting death certificates for 14 military personnel and 5 civilians; Israel declined to produce its own casualties as witnesses.

Rostow told Johnson on 15 November that the "3000-man raid with tanks and planes was out of all proportion to the provocation and was aimed at the wrong target," had "wrecked a good system of tacit cooperation between Hussein and the Israelis," and suggested slowing military deliveries "inconspicuously."

Assistant Secretary Sisco told Ambassador Harman on 15 November that Washington was "dismayed by Israeli attack," feared "this is not the end but the beginning," and expected a "strong resolution" at the UN.

The CIA judged on 18 November that the raid "shattered the modus vivendi" on the border, that about 50 people were killed (half of them soldiers) and about 150 buildings destroyed, that Jordan's army was "clearly humiliated," and that a coup or assassination attempt against Hussein "cannot be ruled out."
Rioting against the Jordanian government followed in the West Bank on a scale beyond any earlier unrest, and Hussein used the army to restore order (GlobalSecurity account).

Resolution 228, adopted on 25 November 1966 by 14 votes to none with New Zealand abstaining and the US voting in favour, censured Israel for "a large-scale and carefully planned military action" in breach of the Charter and the Israel–Jordan armistice and warned that "actions of military reprisal cannot be tolerated."

Johnson wrote to Hussein on 23 November that "Words of sympathy are small comfort when lives have been needlessly destroyed" and ordered an urgent review of how to help; the FRUS editors record that he also warned Israel another such raid would suspend US military shipments.

Jordan's army commander General Khammash then asked Washington for "a stupendous $200 million"; Rostow planned to "whittle" it down, and the FRUS editors record that a military aid package for Jordan was agreed in December 1966.

disputes.question: Why did Israel strike Jordan when Syria was Fatah's patron?

positions.view: Israel's archive presents the raid as a response to the mine attack launched from the West Bank.
Rostow and the CIA judged it disproportionate and aimed at "the wrong target", undermining Hussein, who had kept the border quiet.

disputes.question: How many were killed?

positions.view: UNTSO: 3 civilians and 15 soldiers in its totals, with certificates for 5 civilians and 14 soldiers.
CIA, 18 November: about 50 killed, half of them soldiers.

disputes.question: Who laid the mine, and when?

positions.view: IDF archives: a Fatah mine two days before the raid.
CIA memorandum: Israel attributed the 12 November mining to the Palestine Liberation Front.

entries.topic: The end of military government: easing (1963), the decision (1966), abolition on 1 December 1966, and what remained

sources.label: Akevot Institute, "Aims and Means 3: File GL-17005/6" (Israel State Archives file of the Prime Minister's Adviser on Arab Affairs, 1963–69)
"Israel to Abolish Military Rule in Areas Inhabited by Arabs", JTA, 30 June 1966
"Abolition of the Military Governance of Arab-Populated Areas in Israel (1966)", Economic Cooperation Foundation
"Military rule", Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question, Institute for Palestine Studies

claims.text: On 21 October 1963 Prime Minister Eshkol cancelled the general requirement that Arab citizens carry personal travel permits; a directive of 3 November 1963 by Chief of Staff Zvi Tzur created a general permit for most residents of the Triangle and Wadi 'Ara, excluding the Negev and six border villages, cut the Galilee zones from 17 to nine and kept eleven "abandoned villages" closed.
In March 1963 the Military Advocate General, Meir Shamgar, circulated a secret 13-page manual on the Defence (Emergency) Regulations 1945, printed in 30 copies.
At a meeting chaired by the Adviser on Arab Affairs, Shmuel Toledano, on 18 November 1965, nine villages were reviewed for opening; those with unresolved "land issues" stayed closed.
On 12 January 1966 the Prime Minister told the Knesset the government planned to abolish the military government within a year, although the Chief of Staff had argued for keeping it in eased form.

A meeting on 27 February 1966 chaired by the Prime Minister's adviser Isser Harel set the directives: the apparatus would be dismantled while the Defence Regulations stayed in force; enforcement passed to the Israel Police and in some cases the Shin Bet, with a reinforced Shin Bet, new police stations, a police reserve unit for "mixed communities" and a demolition unit for "illegal construction."

JTA reported on 30 June 1966 that the governorships would end on 1 December 1966 for about 150,000 Arab citizens, mainly along the Jordanian border and around Nazareth, and that a special police headquarters for the Arab minority had already been set up.
Eshkol gave the Knesset notice of abolition on 8 November 1966; because the regime rested on military regulations, no legislation was needed to end it (ECF).

After abolition the police, under the Chief of Staff's supervision, were tasked with enforcing the Emergency Regulations (IPS encyclopedia); the regulations that remained included closed areas (Regulation 125), restriction orders (109), police supervision (110), administrative detention (111, replaced in 1979) and deportation (112).
Toledano described the change as mainly "psychological"; a 1963 document on the regime's aims said "the main change is external-psychological that gives a feeling of equality" (Akevot).

disputes.question: Did 1 December 1966 end military rule over Palestinian citizens?

positions.view: Formally yes: the governorships were abolished and powers passed to civilian bodies (JTA; ECF).

The Israel State Archives file shows the Emergency Regulations kept in force and enforcement transferred to the police and Shin Bet, which Toledano himself called a mainly "psychological" change; the IPS encyclopedia places full legal abolition in late 1968.

entries.topic: The crisis opens: the Soviet warning (13 May), Egyptian forces into Sinai, and UNEF's withdrawal (16–19 May 1967)

claims.text: On 13 May 1967 the Soviet Union told Egypt that Israel was massing about 11 brigades to attack Syria, through at least three channels: to Anwar Sadat during a stop in Moscow, and in Cairo through Egyptian intelligence and the Foreign Ministry; Elbahtimy writes that the information "proved to be false."
The Library of Congress Egypt study gives the Soviet warning as Israel having mobilized two brigades on the frontier, after which Nasser sent troops toward the border and Syria followed.

General Muhammad Fawzi, Egypt's chief of staff, visited the Syrian border on 14 May 1967; his 1997 interview at King's College London covers that visit and the Soviet reports, though the catalogue does not state his conclusions.
Israel's cabinet heard on 17 May that Egyptian forces were moving into Sinai and worked on the assumption that the move was mainly for show, not war.

At 22:00 Gaza time on 16 May Brigadier Eiz-El-Din Mokhtar handed the UNEF commander, Maj.-Gen. Indar Jit Rikhye, a letter from General Fawzi saying UAR troops were concentrated in Sinai to act if Israel attacked any Arab country and asking UNEF to withdraw from the observation posts along the border; Fawzi's text read, "I request that you issue your orders to withdraw all these troops immediately."

U Thant replied the same evening that any request must come to him directly from the UAR government and that on receiving it he would "order the withdrawal of all UNEF troops from Gaza and Sinai," informing the General Assembly at the same time.

The formal UAR request, from Foreign Minister Riad, reached U Thant at noon New York time on 18 May: the UAR "has decided to terminate the presence of the United Nations Emergency Force"; he consulted the UNEF Advisory Committee, which did not ask for a General Assembly session, and replied that evening.

On 15 May 1967 UNEF numbered 3,378 personnel from Brazil, Canada, Denmark, India, Norway, Sweden and Yugoslavia; it had been stationed only on the Egyptian side, Israel refusing it on its side of the line.

U Thant argued that UNEF rested on the host country's consent, that a peacekeeping force cannot function without its "continuing consent and co-operation," and that UAR troop movements had already made the force unworkable; he wrote that Hammarskjöld's private 1957 note "cannot affect in any way the basis for the presence of UNEF."

In his report of 19 May U Thant wrote that UNTSO observers had "confirmed the absence of troop concentrations" on both sides of the Syrian line, that statements attributed to senior Israeli officials were "so threatening as to be particularly inflammatory," and that the situation was "more menacing" than at any time since autumn 1956.

On 26 May Kosygin urged Eshkol to "resort to all measures to prevent a military conflict"; Eshkol replied on 1 June that "there were no Israeli concentrations at the Syrian border" and that he had invited the Soviet ambassador to visit the frontier.

Tal treats the Soviet warning as false and its motive as unexplained, and calls Nasser's Sinai deployment a deterrent gesture toward a feared Israeli strike on Syria, his later steps partly forced by how fast UNEF left; Laurens likewise reads the 14 May deployment as deterrence.
Laurens writes that on 17 May two Egyptian reconnaissance aircraft overflew Dimona undetected.

disputes.question: Why did Moscow send a false warning?

positions.view: Ginor and Remez (as summarized by Elbahtimy) portray the USSR manipulating events toward war.
Elbahtimy, from Egyptian minutes and testimony, finds Moscow a force for restraint, taken aback by events; the false report may still have set off the chain that led to Tiran.
Tal: the warning was false and its motive remains unexplained.

disputes.question: What did Nasser intend by moving into Sinai and removing UNEF?

positions.view: Deterrence on Syria's behalf, escalating partly because UNEF left faster than expected (Tal, Laurens, Library of Congress).
Fawzi's letter of 16 May itself framed the troops as ready to act against Israel if it attacked any Arab country, and Nasser's later speeches went further (see the next entry).

disputes.question: Dates of the UNEF request

positions.view: UN record: Fawzi's letter 16 May; formal UAR request 18 May.
Fanack gives 19 May; the Library of Congress gives 16 May; GlobalSecurity gives 18 May.

claims.text: In a speech to the armed forces on 22 May 1967 Nasser said "The Aqaba Gulf constitutes our Egyptian territorial waters" and "Under no circumstances will we allow the Israeli flag to pass through the Aqaba Gulf," claimed Israel had decided "to carry out an aggression against Syria as of May 17," and said "we are ready for war."

U Thant learned of the Tiran restrictions en route to Cairo, where he stayed from the afternoon of 23 May to 25 May; his report records Israel's position that closing the Strait to Israeli ships, or restricting cargoes bound for Israel, would be a casus belli, and its claim of a right of innocent passage against the UAR's claim of territorial waters.

Israel's cabinet on 23 May defined the blockade as aggression but reached no consensus on a military response and gave diplomacy time; on 26 May it could not agree whether to act; an all-night session on 27 May weighed foreign leaders' appeals for restraint without agreeing a plan.

Fanack records Rabin calling the blockade a "to be or not to be" issue and military intelligence chief Aharon Yariv warning Eshkol that Egyptian forces in Sinai had moved to an offensive posture; Tal records that on 22 May Rabin saw no sign Nasser intended war.

On 26 May Johnson told Eban that "our best judgment is that no military attack on Israel is imminent," McNamara citing three intelligence groups that judged the Egyptian deployments defensive; Johnson called closing the Strait illegal, said "Israel will not be alone unless it decides to go it alone," and stressed "Constitutional processes" and the need for congressional support.

Nasser told Arab trade unionists on 26 May: "The battle will be a general one and our basic objective will be to destroy Israel," and said Egypt could tell UNEF to leave "within half an hour"; the Library of Congress study notes that he publicly denied Egypt would strike first, while Amer and Shams Badran reportedly urged him to.

In Moscow on 26 May Kosygin told Egypt's defense minister Shams Badran, according to Egyptian minutes, "Politically, you prevailed. Militarily you prevailed"; Elbahtimy reads the Egyptian record as Moscow urging restraint.
On 30 May Hussein signed a military alliance with Egypt that placed the Jordanian army under the field command of an Egyptian general officer.

Moshe Dayan became defense minister on 1 June 1967; that day Dayan and Menachem Begin attended a cabinet meeting for the first time, before being sworn in, and Laurens describes the result as a unity government.

On 1 June Meir Amit told McNamara that Israel's mobilization of about 100,000 people was straining the economy, that "time is very much against Israel," that the Soviet claim of a planned attack on Syria was a "sheer fabrication," and estimated about 4,000 casualties in a Sinai campaign; McNamara promised to convey his views to the President.
Amit later said (1992) that he told McNamara he would personally recommend action and that McNamara replied "the president knows that you are here"; the contemporary US record notes no such exchange.

Johnson wrote to Eshkol on 3 June that the US was pursuing a maritime powers' declaration on passage through Tiran, repeated "Israel will not be alone unless it decides to go alone," and urged Israel "not to make itself responsible for the initiation of hostilities."

On 4 June the ministerial defense committee, meeting with the rest of the government, decided "to take military action to free Israel from the suffocating aggression grip tightening around it" (IDF archives); the published decision authorized "the Prime Minister and the Minister of Defence to take steps necessary for the protection of Israel."
Laurens cites Rusk's telegram of 3 June describing an "apocalypse psychology" on both sides and argues the war came from mutual miscalculation, not a deliberate trap by either side.

disputes.question: Did Israel face an imminent attack in late May 1967?

positions.view: Israeli ministers feared being struck first ("If we will not be the first to strike, Nasser will eliminate us", quoted by Tal); Yariv warned of an offensive Egyptian posture; Nasser spoke publicly of destroying Israel.
US intelligence told Eban no attack was imminent and the deployments were defensive; Rabin saw no sign of intent on 22 May; Laurens and Tal read Nasser as practising deterrence and brinkmanship.

disputes.question: Did Washington give a "green light"?

positions.view: The written record is cautionary: Johnson's 26 May words and 3 June letter urge Israel not to initiate hostilities.
Amit's later account and the historians cited by Elbahtimy speak of an "amber" light from his 1 June visit.

disputes.question: Was Tiran actually closed?

positions.view: Nasser announced it on 22 May and Israel treated it as a casus belli (UN record).
The Library of Congress Egypt study says he never carried out the threat.
